summary: Before every flight the PIC checks weather, route, equipment, airworthiness, load, fuel with a margin, and performance, then briefs passengers on exits, belts, and oxygen or life jackets if carried. In flight, everyone obeys the commander, a pilot stays at the controls, and nobody flies impaired (20 mg alcohol per 100 ml of blood; at least 8 hours after drinking). Towing, dropping and parachuting need CofA or CAA approval. Carry the documents Part-NCO lists, or leave items 2 to 8 on the ground for an A-to-A flight. Know the squawks (7700, 7600, 7500, 7000), report an Airprox by radio and confirm within 7 days, and know the equipment rules for over-water flight and oxygen.
sections: Operational rules (UK ANO and Part-NCO)

ICAO Annex 6 (international GA) differs in places from the ANO, so the ANO rules come first, then the Annex 6 extracts for international flights. Air operations: Regulation (EU) 965/2012 (Part-NCO for private flights in other-than-complex aircraft).
Pre-flight actions of the PIC (NCO.GEN.105, ANO Articles 69 and 75)
Before each flight, be satisfied that:
– the flight can be made safely, with the latest route, aerodrome and weather information, and options if it can't be completed as planned
– required equipment (including radio) is carried and working, with suitable maps, charts and navigation equipment
– the aircraft is fit to fly, with a valid ARC or Certificate of Maintenance Review where needed
– the load is safe for weight, distribution and security
– there is enough fuel, oil, coolant (and ballast), with a margin
– performance allows a safe take-off, climb, cruise and landing at the destination
– all pre-flight checks are done
Rough take-off distance factors (use the aircraft's charts for real numbers):
– 10% more weight → about 20% more take-off distance
– tailwind of 10% of lift-off speed (about 5 kt) → about 20% more
– 10°C warmer or 1,000 ft higher → about 10% more
Passenger briefing (ANO Article 73)
Before take-off, brief passengers on emergency exits, seat belts or harnesses, and oxygen and life jackets when carried.
In flight
Commander's authority (Article 244): everyone on board must obey the commander's lawful commands for safety.
Crew composition (Article 66): must meet the rules of the State of Registry.

Pilots at the controls (Article 70): one pilot at the controls at all times; both during take-off and landing if two are required; belt or harness worn at the controls (harness for take-off and landing when one is fitted).
Carriage of persons: nobody in a part of the aircraft not designed for people, or on anything towed, except brief access for safety or to a designed cargo area.
Smoking (Article 243): obey no-smoking signs; the commander can ban it at any time.

Alcohol (Article 242): not drunk on board; crew not impaired by drink or drugs. Legal limit 20 mg per 100 ml of blood (a quarter of the England and Wales driving limit). Rule of thumb: at least 8 hours "bottle to throttle", more after heavy drinking.
Disruptive behaviour (Article 245) and endangering aircraft, people or property recklessly or negligently (Articles 240-241) are offences, e.g. flying dangerously low or with too little fuel.
Radio (Article 79): the operator needs an R/T licence and the radio its own licence.
Flight recorders (Article 231): aeroplanes over 5,700 kg and helicopters over 2,700 kg in some cases.
Towing, dropping and parachuting
Towing gliders (Article 87) and towing or picking up people or articles (Article 88): only if the CofA expressly allows it. Part-SPO covers the EASA rules.
Dropping articles or animals (Article 89): never so as to endanger anyone; otherwise only with CAA written approval, except e.g. life-saving equipment or jettisoning in an emergency.
Dropping persons (Article 90): except escaping in an emergency, only with CAA written permission, a CofA that allows it, and the Parachuting Manual.
Weapons (Article 98): operator's consent, unloaded, not accessible to passengers.
Munitions of war: CAA written permission.

Dangerous goods (Article 97, NCO.GEN.140): harmless items on the ground can be dangerous at altitude in a small cabin (aerosols, lighters, gas cylinders, batteries, fire lighters). If in doubt, leave it out. Mobile phones off before engine start; portable electronic devices: NCO.GEN.125.
Balloons, kites, airships and winch launches (Articles 92-93)
A captive balloon or kite must not fly higher than 60 m agl, within 60 m of a vessel, vehicle or structure, or within an ATZ.
A balloon over 2 m in any dimension must not fly in notified controlled airspace.
Gliders and parascending parachutes: no winch or ground-tow launch above 60 m agl. The CAA can vary any of these in writing.
Documents to be carried (NCO.GEN.135, ANO Article 229)
Aircraft Flight Manual (or equivalent)
Original certificate of registration
Original CofA
Noise certificate, if applicable
List of specific approvals, if applicable
Aircraft radio licence
Insurance certificate
Journey log
Details of the filed flight plan, if applicable
Current, suitable charts for the route and likely diversions
Interception procedures and visual signals
MEL, if applicable
Anything else pertinent to the flight
Taking off and landing at the same aerodrome (staying in UK airspace): items 2 to 8 may stay on the ground.
Non-Part-21 aircraft within the UK: only navigation charts are required.
Using a Part-FCL licence: carry the licence and photo ID (passport or driving licence), and your medical.
Production of documents (Article 235)

Within a reasonable time of a request from an authorised person (police, CAA, Secretary of State), produce the registration and airworthiness certificates, crew licences, personal logbooks (up to 2 years after the last entry), and other documents that should be carried.
Offences (Article 256)

Using a forged, altered, revoked or suspended document, or one you're not entitled to; lending one with intent to deceive; forging, defacing or falsifying a logbook or record, or destroying it while it must be kept. Entries in ink or indelible pencil.
SSR transponders
Mode A: 4,096 four-digit codes.
Mode C: adds pressure altitude (from an encoding altimeter).
Mode S: individual aircraft address and identity, better detection.

The book's carriage rules are the old Mode A/C ones. Today the UK AIP (ENR 1.6) requires Mode S at and above FL100, in Transponder Mandatory Zones (TMZs) and in much controlled airspace; check ENR 1.6.
Where not mandatory, squawk 7000 with ALT (Mode C) unless ATC gives you a code.
Without a transponder, expect not to be let into a TMZ.
7700: Emergency (keep an assigned code if already in contact with a unit)
7600: Radio failure
7500: Unlawful interference
7000: VFR conspicuity
2000: IFR conspicuity / no code assigned
7004: Aerobatics and display
0033: Parachute dropping (from 5 minutes before until parachutists are down)
0030: Lost (UK)
Select Mode C with all of them. Don't pass through 7500/7600/7700 when changing codes.
Airprox

If you think your aircraft was endangered by another aircraft's proximity, report an Airprox: first by radio to the ATSU you're talking to (or by phone after landing, preferably to an ACC), then confirm within 7 days online on CA Form 1094. AIP ENR 1.14.
International flights (ICAO Annex 6)
Obey the laws of each State you fly in. The PIC is responsible for the operation and safety of the aeroplane and everyone on board.
If an emergency forces you to break local rules, tell the authority as soon as possible (some want a report within 10 days).
Accident with serious injury, death or substantial damage: the PIC notifies the authority as quickly as possible.
Carry search and rescue information for the areas overflown (recommended).
Before flight, check facilities (aerodromes, communications, navaids) are adequate; don't fly below aerodrome operating minima.
Brief crew and passengers on seat belts, exits, life jackets, oxygen and other emergency equipment, including life rafts.
Aeroplane airworthy, registered, certificates on board, suitable instruments, maintenance done, mass and balance in limits, cargo secured, Flight Manual limits respected.

VFR: don't start unless current reports and forecasts show VMC along the route; don't continue unless the destination or an alternate is at or above minima. No flight into known icing without suitable equipment.
Enough fuel and oil for the weather and expected delays.
Report weather or hazards (volcanic ash, dust storms) likely to affect other flights.
Taxiing: only if authorised, competent, radio-qualified where needed, and briefed on the aerodrome's layout, signs and procedures.
Refuelling with passengers on board: only with the PIC or a qualified person ready to organise an evacuation.
Part-NCO aeroplanes
First-aid kit, kept up to date
At least one hand fire extinguisher
Spare fuses (if fuses, not circuit breakers)
A seat and seat belt for each person (above an age set by the State)

ELT: any type if the first CofA was on or before 1 July 2008; an automatic ELT if later; or, for aircraft with six seats or fewer, a survival ELT or PLB carried by someone on board. They transmit on 121.5 MHz and 406 MHz.
Instruments
VFR by day: magnetic heading, time (hours, minutes, seconds), pressure altitude, indicated airspeed.

VFR at night (or where instruments are needed to hold a flight path), also: turn and slip, attitude, vertical speed, stabilised heading, and a warning when gyro power is inadequate. Where instruments are needed: pitot heat.
Over water (Part-NCO)

Single-engine aeroplanes: a life jacket for each person (or a flotation device for those under 24 months) when beyond gliding distance from land, or taking off or landing where the path over water makes a ditching likely. In a single, wear it (uninflated).

More than 30 minutes at cruise or 50 nm from land suitable for an emergency landing, whichever is less: the PIC assesses the survival risk and decides on life rafts, distress signals and life-saving equipment.
ICAO Annex 6 (book): life rafts beyond 100 nm (single-engine) or 200 nm (multi-engine).
Areas where search and rescue would be especially difficult: signalling and survival equipment.
Oxygen (unpressurised)
Crew: continuously above 10,000 ft for more than 30 minutes, and at all times above 13,000 ft.
Passengers: above 13,000 ft.

sum.Operational rules (UK ANO and Part-NCO): ANO rules first, then ICAO Annex 6 for international flights; Part-NCO covers private flights.
sum.Pre-flight actions of the PIC (NCO.GEN.1: Weather, equipment, airworthiness, load, fuel with a margin, performance and checks, before every flight.
sum.Passenger briefing (ANO Article 73): Exits, belts or harnesses, and oxygen and life jackets when carried.
sum.In flight: Obey the commander, a pilot at the controls, belts on, no drink or drugs.
sum.Towing, dropping and parachuting: Only if the CofA or the CAA allows it; never endanger people or property.
sum.Balloons, kites, airships and winch laun: Captive balloons and kites: 60 m agl, 60 m from structures, not in an ATZ.
sum.Documents to be carried (NCO.GEN.135, AN: Thirteen items under Part-NCO; for an A-to-A flight items 2 to 8 can stay on the ground.
sum.Production of documents (Article 235): Produce certificates, licences and logbooks to an authorised person within a reasonable time.
sum.Offences (Article 256): Forging, lending or falsifying documents and logbooks is an offence.
sum.SSR transponders: 7700 emergency, 7600 radio failure, 7500 unlawful interference, 7000 conspicuity; select ALT.
sum.Airprox: Report by radio straight away and confirm within 7 days on CA1094.
sum.International flights (ICAO Annex 6): Obey local law, check facilities and minima, VMC along the route, enough fuel, report hazards.
sum.Part-NCO aeroplanes: First-aid kit, fire extinguisher, seats and belts, and an ELT or PLB.
sum.Instruments: Day VFR: compass heading, time, pressure altitude, airspeed. Night adds attitude, turn and slip, VSI, heading.
sum.Over water (Part-NCO): Life jackets beyond gliding distance; beyond 30 minutes or 50 nm the PIC decides on rafts.
sum.Oxygen (unpressurised): Crew above 10,000 ft for over 30 minutes and always above 13,000 ft; passengers above 13,000 ft.

quiz.q: Before take-off the pilot-in-command must brief passengers on:
o: Emergency exits, seat belts or harnesses, and oxygen and life jackets if carried
Emergency exits only, since the other items are covered by placards in the cabin
Seat belts or harnesses, and the aircraft's performance and planned route
The route, the weather, and the expected time of arrival at the destination
quiz.why: ANO Article 73: exits, belts or harnesses, and oxygen and life jackets when they are carried.

quiz.q: The legal blood alcohol limit for a pilot is:
o: 20 mg per 100 ml of blood
80 mg per 100 ml of blood
50 mg per 100 ml of blood
9 mg per 100 ml of blood
quiz.why: 20 mg, a quarter of the England and Wales drink-driving limit of 80 mg.

quiz.q: The transponder code for radio failure is:
quiz.why: 7600 is radio failure; 7700 emergency; 7500 unlawful interference; 7000 conspicuity.

quiz.q: Below FL100 a VFR pilot should squawk 7000 with ALT unless:
o: ATC has assigned a code, or a special-purpose code applies
You are flying in Class G airspace and outside any ATZ or MATZ
The flight visibility is more than 10 km in VMC
The aircraft has a Mode S transponder with ADS-B
quiz.why: Use 7000 unless you have been given a code or need a special one (emergency, lost, parachuting, aerobatics).

quiz.q: An Airprox reported by radio must be confirmed:
o: Within 7 days on CA Form 1094
Within 24 hours by phone to the CAA
Within 28 days in writing to the CAA
Only if the ATC unit asks you to
quiz.why: Report by radio at once, then confirm within 7 days online (CA1094).

quiz.q: The final authority for the safe conduct of a flight rests with:
o: The pilot-in-command
The aircraft operator
The person at the controls
ATC in controlled airspace
quiz.why: Annex 6 and the ANO: the PIC. The person at the controls may not be the PIC, and ATC never takes over that authority.

quiz.q: A pilot plans a local flight, taking off and landing at the same aerodrome within the UK, in a Part-21 aeroplane. Which document may stay on the ground?
o: The certificate of insurance
The aircraft Flight Manual
Current charts
The interception procedures
quiz.why: Items 2 to 8 (registration, CofA, noise certificate, approvals, radio licence, insurance, journey log) may stay at the aerodrome. The Flight Manual, charts and interception procedures still fly.

ref.sec: Documents to be carried (NCO.GEN.135, ANO Article 229)

quiz.q: A captive balloon or kite must not be flown:
o: Higher than 60 m agl, within 60 m of a structure, or inside an ATZ
Higher than 150 m agl, within 150 m of a structure, or inside an ATZ
Higher than 60 m agl, within 60 m of a structure, or inside a CTR
Higher than 60 m agl, within 600 m of a congested area, or in an ATZ
quiz.why: All three limits apply: 60 m agl, 60 m from vessels, vehicles or structures, and not in an ATZ.

ref.sec: Balloons, kites, airships and winch launches (Articles 92-93)

quiz.q: Under Part-NCO, a single-engine aeroplane flying further from land than 30 minutes at cruise or 50 nm (whichever is less):
o: The PIC must assess the survival risk and decide on life rafts and distress signals
Must carry a life raft with enough places for everyone on board, whatever the assessed risk
Needs no extra equipment provided everyone on board wears a life jacket
Must file a flight plan with D&D and carry a personal locator beacon
quiz.why: Part-NCO leaves the raft decision to the PIC's risk assessment beyond 30 minutes or 50 nm. The book's 100 nm raft rule is ICAO Annex 6.

quiz.q: In an unpressurised aeroplane the crew must use oxygen:
o: Above 10,000 ft for more than 30 minutes, and at all times above 13,000 ft
At all times above 10,000 ft, and for more than 30 minutes above 8,000 ft
Above 13,000 ft for more than 30 minutes, and at all times above 15,000 ft
Above 8,000 ft at night, and at all times above 10,000 ft by day
quiz.why: The 30-minute allowance applies between 10,000 and 13,000 ft; above 13,000 ft oxygen is needed all the time.
